repairs.after: Raw material. Two disputes. A service reports mean request time of 100ms; a user reports her mean wait is 1s. A service reports MTTR under 1 minute; a user reports mean outage length of 1 hour. Both sides are right. The operator counts events (one request, one outage); the customer samples elapsed time, and the number of times a customer hits a given outage is proportional to that outage's length. This is the inspection paradox: customers do not see f(t), they see a t-weighted version. If the operator's mean is E[X], the customer-experienced mean is E_a[X] = E[X^2] / (2 E[X]) = 0.5 * (E[X] + Var(X)/E[X]). The gap is proportional to Var(X)/E[X], and Var(X) is often very large relative to E[X]. Fitted log-normal example: median TTR 30 minutes, p99 600 minutes (10 hours, one event in 100) gives MTTR just over 1 hour (about 69 minutes) and, from that same formula, a customer-experienced mean of about 3 hours (about 180 minutes). A simulator uses lognormal failure_mu=1.0, failure_sigma=3.0, Poisson client arrivals at rate 100, 1000 samples. Timeout-and-retry can hide some service-time tail, but nothing hides recovery-time tail. Write a design doc for a platform org proposing how availability and recovery should be measured.
repairs.rationale: Kept the formula, fixed the number. The formula is the load-bearing object: it is graded at q2, it is the identity that makes the brief's Var(X)/E[X] point work, and it is exactly what the brief's own simulator computes (brooker-waiting.txt:67, mean(square(server_saw_times))/(2.0*mean(server_saw_times))). The 6-hour figure was the length-biased mean, a different statistic answering a different question. Recomputed: mu=ln(30)=3.4011974, sigma=(ln600-ln30)/2.3263479=1.2877405. E[X]=exp(mu+s^2/2)=68.740 min=1.146 h (the brief's 'just over 1 hour' holds). E[X^2]=exp(2mu+2s^2)=24808.60. E[X^2]/(2E[X])=180.452 min=3.008 h. Cross-check of the identity: 0.5*(E[X]+Var/E[X])=180.452 min, exact agreement. The discarded 6-hour value is E[X^2]/E[X]=360.903 min=6.015 h, which also equals exp(mu+s^2+s^2/2)=360.903, i.e. the lognormal length-biased mean. I added the explicit minute values so the agreement between printed formula and printed number is checkable on the page rather than only in a reviewer's head. The simulator's clients record this_outage - t, the residual, so 3 hours is also what that code produces; the brief is now consistent with both its formula and its simulator.

repairs.before: Raw material. Concurrency control choice in Aurora DSQL. Optimistic concurrency control is credited with a practical advantage beyond throughput: clients can never block other clients. At scale, performance cross talk between clients is a significant contributor to tail latency in applications backed by pessimistic relational databases; the canonical case is a client that pauses for garbage collection while holding a write lock. Operational experience at Amazon: contention on locks, and retries after failing to acquire locks, are frequent contributors to system outages and to metastable failures that drive long recovery times. Avoiding that class of failure, plus more mundane failures caused by misbehaving clients and client code, was a design objective. Figure 6 of the paper reports SELECT and UPDATE latencies that stay fast even in the multi-region configuration. Separate thread: the 2007 Amazon Dynamo paper's embrace of eventual consistency, and Werner Vogels' 2009 article Eventually Consistent, reflected the belief that cloud-scale systems had to accept eventual consistency to hit availability and latency goals. Since then, advances in time distribution, data-center networking, power and cooling infrastructure, and distributed protocols have moved those trade-offs. The position taken: strong consistency is the right default and the right choice for nearly all applications. Write a design doc justifying the concurrency-control and consistency defaults for a new transactional datastore.
repairs.after: Raw material. Concurrency control in Aurora DSQL, a multi-region relational database. Optimistic concurrency control was chosen for throughput and for one isolation property: under it a client is never in a position to block another one. Claimed consequence at scale: client-to-client performance cross talk, a large driver of tail latency whenever an application sits on a pessimistic relational engine. Stock illustration: a process stops for garbage collection holding a write lock, and everything queued behind it stops too. Operational record from Amazon: lock contention, and the retries that follow a failed lock acquisition, turn up repeatedly as causes of outages and of metastable failure, with long recoveries. Two design objectives follow: keep applications out of metastable failure, and blunt the duller failures that come from badly behaved clients and client code. Measured result: figure 6 plots SELECT and UPDATE latency, and both stay fast even with the database running across regions. Second thread, consistency defaults. Two publications from the 2000s, the Amazon Dynamo paper (2007) and Werner Vogels' article Eventually Consistent (2009), held that cloud-scale systems had to give up strong consistency to reach their availability and latency targets. Four things have shifted since: how time is distributed, how data-centre networks are built, how power and cooling are provisioned, and what distributed protocols can do. Position taken: strong consistency now belongs as the default, and almost no application is better served by eventual consistency. Write a design doc justifying the concurrency-control and consistency defaults for a new transactional datastore.

The closing verbatim clause is gone: the string 'is the right default, and the right choice for nearly all applications' no longer appears, so the brief no longer hands every condition the recorded human_last_words for the graded span; the same position is now stated as 'strong consistency now belongs as the default, and almost no application is better served by eventual consistency'. Every fact the five questions grade is still present and now carried in the brief's own words: cross talk and its pessimistic-engine scope (q1), figure 6 (q2), lock contention plus retries plus metastability (q3), the four areas of advance (q4), misbehaving clients and client code (q5). The ask is unchanged: the source is Brooker justifying OCC and strong consistency, and 'write a design doc justifying the concurrency-control and consistency defaults' is the matching genre, so condition H stays a fair comparator.
